captions.instagram:
How does an octopus change color?

An octopus can repaint its whole body in a fraction of a second. Its skin is a screen of thousands of tiny pigment bags, each pulled open by its own ring of muscles on orders from the brain. Fire the nerves and watch the pixels open.

→ An octopus has eight arms, three hearts and about 500 million nerve cells, most of them in its arms.
→ Each colour spot is a sac of pigment. When its nerve fires, a ring of muscles pulls it wide open.
→ Thousands of sacs switch patterns in about a quarter of a second. A chameleon needs a minute or two.
→ On gravel it mottles. On big rocks it goes disruptive, breaking up its own outline.
→ The mimic octopus hides six arms and waves two banded ones, like a venomous sea snake.

youtubeLong.title: How does an octopus change color? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
An octopus can repaint its whole body in a fraction of a second. Its skin is a screen of thousands of tiny pigment bags, each pulled open by its own ring of muscles on orders from the brain. Fire the nerves and watch the pixels open.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/octopusclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/octopusclear

In this video:
• Eight arms and a living screen. A common octopus has a soft mantle, eight sucker-lined arms, a siphon, slit-pupil eyes and about 500 million nerve cells, two-thirds of them in its arms.
• Pixels with muscles. Each chromatophore is an elastic bag of yellow, red or brown pigment ringed by radial muscles wired to the brain.
• Three disguises, and some acts. Most camouflage is uniform, mottle or disruptive, chosen from the size, contrast and edges of things nearby.
• Colour-blind, yet colour-matching. Octopus eyes have one kind of light sensor, so they should be colour-blind.
• Cousins, catches and care. Cuttlefish and squid use the same muscle-driven cells.
• How we found out. Aristotle saw octopuses match stones; Sangiovanni named the chromatophores in 1819; J.
